blocks.text: Bacon!
Ranked!

37.1 grams of fat. The bright spot is 5.8 grams of polyunsaturated fat, which helps balance the fat profile. The pressure point is 12.6 grams of saturated fat. For meats, fat quality matters because the protein can be good, but the fat decides how clean the tradeoff feels.
Carbs are basically out of the picture here. There are no defensible carb submacros to score, so this section does not really help or hurt bacon in the way it would for grains, fruits, or tubers.

13.7 grams of protein. Essential amino acids land at 9 out of 9, so the protein has a real repair and maintenance role. Non-essential amino acids are also strong at 10 out of 11, while collagen is only 0.4 grams. For meats, protein quality is the main reason this entry stays interesting.

Vitamin B12 is the clear vitamin mark at 21% daily value, supporting nerves and blood cells. Vitamin D is only 1% daily value, and the rest of the vitamin panel is thin, so bacon is not carrying the broad micronutrient workload you might want from a meat.
Zinc is the best mineral mark at 10% daily value, with a modest immune-support angle. Iron is only 2% daily value and potassium is 4%, so the mineral section is mostly weak for a meat entry.

Pros first: highly palatable and appealing. It is an obvious reason people like it. works as a strong flavour booster. A small amount can carry a whole plate. has strong comfort-food appeal. It is instantly recognisable and easy to package in meals.

The drawbacks next: sodium is a major drawback. Even a small serving can bring a lot of salt, so it adds up fast. processing is a major negative. Because bacon is cured meat, the health tradeoff is bigger than the macro numbers alone suggest. salty, fatty flavour makes portions easy to overdo. That flavour is part of the appeal, but it also makes bacon harder to keep as a small add-on.

So Bacon has real protein quality, useful vitamin B12, and a strong flavour role. But saturated fat, low vitamin D, low iron, heavy sodium, processing, and portions that are easy to overdo pull it down hard. It is best as a small flavour tool or occasional comfort-food add-on, not as a core everyday protein.
D tier.

Ranked!
-

-

-

-

-

episode.narrationText:
Chicken Thigh!
-
Ranked!
-
8 grams of fat. Saturated fat is 2.3 grams, supporting a cleaner fat profile. Omega 3 is 70 milligrams, weak for omega-3 fat support, and for meats, fat quality is a major tradeoff. For meats, fat quality matters a lot once the protein is already there.
-
No defensible carb submacros to call out. In this category, carbs barely matter.
-
24 grams of protein. Essential amino acids score is 9 out of 9, making the protein useful for repair and maintenance. Collagen is only 0.8 grams, weak for connective-tissue protein, so for meats, it is not bringing much connective-tissue protein. Strong protein is expected here, so the rest of the profile decides how high it climbs.
-
Vitamin B12 is 12% daily value, useful for nerve and blood-cell support. Vitamin D is only 0% daily value, weak for bone and immune support, which is a small miss for meats.
-
Zinc is 14% daily value, useful for immune support. Iron is only 5% daily value, weak for oxygen transport, which is a weak mark for meats.
-
Pros first: dark meat stays flavorful and forgiving to cook. That makes chicken thigh easier to use well in real meals than drier leaner cuts. Usually a reasonably affordable whole-food protein. Chicken thigh is often cheaper than premium animal proteins while still providing a substantial protein serving. Easy to build complete meals around. It works as an actual centrepiece protein rather than a garnish ingredient.
-
Cons next: fattier than lean poultry options like breast meat. That tradeoff is part of why thigh tastes better but is not the cleanest poultry profile. The final health profile changes a lot with cooking method. Breading, deep frying, or skin-on preparation can shift the outcome substantially from this base record. Raw poultry needs careful handling. Food-safety friction is a practical downside versus foods that are safer or easier to store and prep.
-
Big strengths are protein, dark meat stays flavorful and forgiving to cook, and usually a reasonably affordable whole-food protein, but the biggest weaknesses are low iron, low vitamin D, and low omega 3. It is good for muscles and strength sports, practical meals, and blood and oxygen support because the protein section supports repair and maintenance, the food-type role makes it easy to build meals around, and vitamin B12 supports the blood-and-oxygen side.
-
C tier.

episode.narrationText:
Extra Virgin Olive Oil!
-
Ranked!
-
100 grams of fat. Cholesterol is 0 milligrams, keeping the fat tradeoff lighter. Omega 3 is 760 milligrams, supporting a more useful fat profile, but it is the softer support mark in this section. For this category, the real question is fat quality.
-
No defensible carb submacros to call out. Not relevant here.
-
No defensible protein submacros to call out. Also not relevant here.
-
Vitamin E is 93% daily value, adding useful vitamin support. Vitamin A is only 0% daily value, weak for vision and immune support, which is a weak mark for oils and fats.
-
Iron is 3% daily value, the best mark here but still too low to carry the section. Magnesium is only 0% daily value, weak for mineral support, which is a weak mark for oils and fats.
-
Positives first: fresh EVOO can bring polyphenols. The bitter, peppery quality is part of the real extra-virgin advantage. Mostly monounsaturated fat identity. That gives it a different fat-quality role from many seed oils and animal fats. Helps carry fat-soluble nutrients. A little oil can make vegetable-heavy meals work better.
-
Downsides next: quality drops with heat, light, and age. The best part of extra virgin olive oil depends on freshness and storage. Extremely energy dense. It is still pure fat, so the calories arrive fast. Easy to overpour without noticing. Free-pouring can quietly add a lot more than intended.
-
Big strengths are fat quality, vitamin E, and fresh EVOO can bring polyphenols, but the biggest weaknesses are low magnesium, quality drops with heat, light, and age, and extremely energy dense. It is good for hormone health, heart health, and cooking use because fat quality is its main useful job when portions are controlled, unsaturated fats and polyphenols make the heart-health angle clearer, and the fat section is the main job and the use case depends on controlled portions.
-
S tier.

episode.narrationText:
Sweet Potato!
-
Ranked!
-
0.1 grams of fat. Saturated fat is 0 grams, supporting a cleaner fat profile. Omega 3 is 5 milligrams, weak for omega-3 fat support, which is a weak mark for tubers. For a tuber, the cleanest win is a more stable carb profile.
-
20.1 grams of carbs. Glycemic index is 44 GI, helping with steadier carb behaviour. Fibre is 3 grams, weak for digestion and steadier meals, which is a meaningful miss for tubers. For tubers, the carb side decides whether the food feels stable or flimsy.
-
1.6 grams of protein. So protein is barely part of the case. Essential amino acids score is 0 out of 9, weak for repair-and-maintenance protein quality, which is a weak mark for tubers. Protein is usually limited here, so the other sections have to carry more.
-
Vitamin A is 160% daily value, useful for vision and immune support. Vitamin C is only 3% daily value, weak for collagen formation and antioxidant support, which is a weak mark for tubers.
-
Potassium is 10% daily value, useful for fluid balance. Iron is only 3% daily value, weak for oxygen transport, which is a weak mark for tubers.
-
The upsides first: beta-carotene is the signature upside. The orange flesh gives sweet potato a clear carotenoid identity. Better fibre support than many tubers. The fibre helps the carb package look more useful. Naturally sweet without added sugar. It brings sweetness without needing a processed dessert format.
-
The drawbacks next: glycemic impact changes with cooking method. Baking, boiling, cooling, and mashing can change the real-world carb behaviour. Large portions push carbs up fast. It is still a starchy tuber, so the carb load can climb quickly. Protein is barely part of the case. The tuber job is energy and carotenoids, not meaningful protein.
-
Big strengths are fibre, vitamin A, and beta-carotene is the signature upside, but the biggest weaknesses are low iron, low protein quality, and low omega 3. It is good for immune support, practical meals, and digestion because vitamin A gives the immune-support side a reason to exist, the food-type role makes it easy to build meals around, and fibre supports digestion and steadier meals.
-
S tier.

Watermelon Seeds (Unsalted)!
-
Ranked!
-
47.4 grams of fat. Polyunsaturated fat is 14.6 grams, the best mark here but still only modest support. Omega 3 is 90 milligrams, weak for omega-3 fat support, and for seeds, fat quality has to justify the calories. For seeds, the fat profile is one of the biggest reasons they earn their place.
-
15.3 grams of carbs. Sugar is 0.4 grams, helping keep the sugar load under control. Fibre is 4 grams, weak for digestion and steadier meals, which is a small miss for seeds. For a seed, that is exactly what you want to see.
-
28.3 grams of protein. That amount is useful enough to count. Bioavailability is 74%, helping more of that protein count, but it is the softer support mark in this section. Protein is a bonus, but not enough by itself.
-
Vitamins are low overall. For seeds, vitamin E is the main check, so this section is not adding much.
-
Magnesium is 129% daily value, adding useful mineral support. Calcium is only 5% daily value, weak for bone support, which is a weak mark for seeds.
-
Pros first: easy to sprinkle into meals for a real upgrade. Seeds often shine as support foods. Tiny food with serious nutrient density. Seeds often overperform for their size. Often brings dense micronutrient support. That is part of what makes the category interesting.
-
Cons next: texture or prep can be a barrier. Not everyone uses seeds consistently. Real serving sizes are often small. Some strong paper numbers are hard to cash out in practice. Calorie density still stacks up fast. Tiny foods can still overshoot fast.
-

-

episode.narrationText:
Zucchini!
-
Ranked!
-
0.3 grams of fat. Saturated fat is 0.1 grams, supporting a cleaner fat profile. Omega 3 is 15 milligrams, weak for omega-3 fat support, which is a weak mark for vegetables. For a vegetable, this is all about actual nutritional payoff.
-
3.1 grams of carbs. Glycemic index is 15 GI, helping with steadier carb behaviour. Starch is 0 grams, weak for useful staple-carb payoff, which is a small miss for vegetables. For vegetables, low downside is useful, but there still needs to be real payoff.
-
1.2 grams of protein. Not enough to make protein a serious strength. Essential amino acids score is 0 out of 9, weak for repair-and-maintenance protein quality, which is a weak mark for vegetables. Protein is not the main pitch here, but extra support still matters.
-
Vitamin C is 20% daily value, useful for collagen formation and antioxidant support. Vitamin A is only 4% daily value, weak for vision and immune support, which is a weak mark for vegetables.
-
Potassium is 6% daily value, the best mark here but still too low to carry the section. Calcium is only 1% daily value, weak for bone support, which is a weak mark for vegetables.
-
Pros first: good volume for the calories. That matters for satiety and general usefulness. Helps add volume without much calorie cost. That makes vegetables easier to use often. Easy to build meals around. A practical plus because good foods need realistic use cases.
-
Cons next: texture or flavour can limit repeat use. Strong nutrition still has to survive normal eating habits. Prep can decide whether it actually gets eaten. Vegetables can lose practical value when washing, chopping, or cooking becomes a barrier. Very light profile can feel underpowered. For some vegetables, the practical payoff is more volume and texture than a big nutrient payload.
-
Big strengths are good volume for the calories, helps add volume without much calorie cost, and easy to build meals around, but the biggest weaknesses are low calcium, low vitamin A, and low protein quality. It is good for low-calorie volume, practical meals, and immune support because it can add bulk or fullness without much calorie pressure, the food-type role makes it easy to build meals around, and vitamin C gives the immune-support side a reason to exist.
-
